name: Owen Davies
specialization: Post-Reformation cunning folk; continuity of magical practice after witch trials; popular magic in modern England

major_works.title: Popular Magic: Cunning-folk in English History
major_works.significance: Comprehensive study of cunning folk in England from Reformation to twentieth century; showed continuity of magical practice service after witch-trial era ended

major_works.title: Witchcraft, Magic and Culture 1736-1951
major_works.significance: Post-prosecution popular magical beliefs and their legal and cultural management in modern England

major_works.title: America Bewitched: The Story of Witchcraft After Salem
major_works.significance: Extension of cunning folk analysis to American context; post-Salem popular witchcraft and magic

core_argument: Magical belief and practice did not end with the witch trials; cunning folk continued to operate in England well into the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, serving community needs for healing, divination, and counter-magic. The end of formal prosecution did not indicate the end of belief; it indicated a change in how the state managed popular magic.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Newspaper records, court records for petty offenses related to magic, folklore collection records, parish records from post-1736 England
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Continuity of cunning folk practice after Witchcraft Act 1736; social functions of popular magic; legal and cultural management of magical practitioners
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Archival survey of post-prosecution period; newspaper and court record analysis; continuity across before/after periodization
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Social-functional: magic serving community needs across changing legal and religious contexts

key_contributions.claim: Cunning folk and popular magical practitioners continued operating in England in substantial numbers through the nineteenth century and beyond, demonstrating that legal suppression did not end magical practice
key_contributions.implication: The witch trial period cannot be sharply periodized from what followed; magical belief and practice show long-term continuity

key_contributions.claim: Cunning folk operated as recognized community specialists in healing, lost property recovery, and counter-magic; they were not marginal figures but integrated practitioners
key_contributions.implication: Extends Hutton's social history of cunning folk into the post-prosecution period

key_contributions.claim: After 1736, the state managed popular magic through fraud laws and public health regulation rather than demonological prosecution; the form of control changed but not the attempt to control
key_contributions.implication: State regulation of magical practice is continuous across the prosecution/post-prosecution divide

reception_and_critique.major_influences: Keith Thomas, Ronald Hutton, English social history; folklore studies
criticisms: English focus limits applicability to Continental patterns
The cunning folk tradition may be too specific to English religious culture to generalize
Some argue Davies underweights the changes in magical culture that did occur after the prosecution period

historiographical_significance: Davies established the study of post-prosecution popular magic as a legitimate historical field, demonstrating that 1736 (end of English prosecutions) was not a cultural discontinuity but a legal one. His comprehensive survey of cunning folk extends Ronald Hutton's social history methodology into the modern period and provides essential evidence for long-term continuity of magical culture in England.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
